messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
Marianne was 54, a European American woman who had spent most of her adult life in kitchens, and when she first came for treatment she described herself as still doing the work she knew best but no longer moving through the world in the same way. Before the assault, she had been the kind of chef who could keep several things going at once, calling orders across a hot line and moving through a crowded kitchen with easy authority. The assault happened after work, when she was alone with a man she had known well enough to trust. She had believed she was in a safe, ordinary situation, in a place and with a person that should not have required caution. Instead, she was attacked, and afterward what stayed with her was not a full, orderly story but a series of harsh fragments: the sense of being pinned, the shock of realizing he was the one who had hurt her, and a bodily memory that returned in pieces she could not easily put into words. When she tried to speak about it, she often stopped and said that the event did not come out as a narrative in her mind; it came back as sensations and disconnected flashes that would not fit together into a beginning, middle, and end.

In the weeks and months that followed, Marianne found that certain kinds of conversation now made her tense before she fully noticed it. Discussions that drifted toward assault, betrayal, or women being unsafe would leave her quiet and watchful, as if the topic itself were too close to something unstable. She also became uncomfortable when someone tried to get emotionally close to her. She had once been warm and open with her husband and a few close friends, but now she felt exposed when another person pressed for intimacy or asked her to explain how she was doing. She found herself pulling back, not because she wanted to be alone, but because emotional closeness made her feel as though she were being asked to trust the wrong thing again. Being alone with men was especially difficult. At work, she still managed the kitchen, but she arranged herself so that there were always others around when possible, and she felt uneasy in the practical moments that used to seem ordinary, such as stepping into a storage area with a male line cook or finding herself briefly isolated in a back corridor with a deliveryman. She did not describe herself as irrational; rather, she had come to believe that being careful was the only sensible response, because someone could appear familiar and still be dangerous.

Her daily life became organized around scanning. In the restaurant she was superalert to who was entering the kitchen, where men were standing, and whether anyone was moving unexpectedly near her. A sudden hand reaching past her at the pass, a colleague turning sharply behind her, or an unfamiliar man approaching the front of the restaurant would make her react as if she were in danger before she had time to sort out what was actually happening. She was embarrassed by how quickly her body braced itself, but she could not stop it. Even in ordinary settings, if a stranger approached her in a parking lot, at a store, or near her workplace, she felt threatened in a way that was immediate and hard to shake. Marianne said she was not “looking for trouble,” but she was always on guard for it. That watchfulness had become part of how she crossed a room, checked a doorway, or assessed the people around her.

What troubled her most in the therapy room was how the event lived in her body. When a memory surfaced, it did not arrive as a clear scene that she could tell from start to finish. Instead, she would get disconnected bits—a smell, a position, a flash of the room—and sometimes her body seemed to drop back into the same position it had been in during the assault, as though she were folded into the memory rather than remembering it from a distance. She spoke with frustration about not being able to put the frightening event into words, and she seemed disturbed by how incomplete and physical the recollections felt. This was especially painful because it confirmed what she had come to believe about other people: that someone could be trusted right up until the moment they were not. She often repeated that you can never know who will harm you, and that people cannot be trusted, even those who seem familiar, kind, or ordinary.

By the time she sought help, Marianne was still working, still married, and still managing her responsibilities, but with a narrowed sense of safety and a growing exhaustion from living on alert. Her husband had noticed how guarded she had become, and Marianne herself was tired of the distance that had opened between the life she used to have and the one she now inhabited. What finally brought her in was the fear that she would never again feel comfortable around other people, especially men, or in the close, busy environments that used to define her. She wanted help because she was frightened by how much of her day was spent bracing for harm, and she was hoping, cautiously, to find a way to move through the world without feeling that danger could appear from any stranger, any conversation, or any moment of unexpected closeness.
